title: Shadowscape: Mechanically rich, thematically poor
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7PSt_Gouh6g

Daniel (@dungeondive) looks at *Shadowscape*, set in the *Mistfall* world, and delivers his verdict in the title: mechanically rich, thematically poor. Despite the small box it eats a table: 25 room cards in a 5×5 grid, four Whisper quests, four buyable actions, four items and hero tableaus.

The mechanisms he admires are real. Monsters move by symbols printed on room exits that match their token, never doubling back, a patrol system he likens to *Dungeon Crusade*. Hero actions are double-sided cards that flip when used, so you plan around what the reverse shows. Fate cards boost any action, drive enemy activation, and in co-op are also the timer, so spending them speeds your doom. Damage lands on your hero or on action cards, locking those actions until healed. No dice: an enemy dies only if you deal its whole value at once.

Then the theme. Fate cards have no names, quests are pickup-and-delivery errands, and the art, though good, is random: a desert for a beast lair, a tower for a weapon delivery. Daniel's three ways to marry mechanism and theme are flavour text, art and backstory, and he judges *Shadowscape* misses all three. He suspects an efficiency-minded friend would love it, and admits he is not good enough at this kind of puzzle to do well. Theme is king; the box stays on the shelf for a possible revisit.

----

Names on cards are the cheapest theme there is. Which game hooked you with nothing more than good names, and which lost you without them?
